propositions.text: The claimants are Guatemalan citizens seeking protection under Canadian immigration law.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, her husband XXXX XXXX XXXX and their son XXXX XXXX XXXX are citizens of Guatemala. They are claiming protection in Canada under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the claimants are Guatemalan citizens seeking protection under Canadian immigration law.

propositions.text: The mother was appointed as the designated representative of her son.
propositions.quote: The mother, Ms. XXXX XXXX, was appointed as the designated representative of her son.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the mother was appointed as the designated representative of her son.

propositions.text: The female claimant was a vendor affected by organized crime involving police commanders, political officials, and customs officers.
propositions.quote: The female claimant was a vendor of XXXX XXXX and XXXX. Organized crime complicated her activities on the street. The female claimant alleged that several police commanders, political officials and customs officers were involved.

propositions.text: These officials lived off corruption and impunity profits.
propositions.quote: They lived off the profits of corruption and impunity.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges organized crime involving officials affected her vending activities and they profited from corruption and impunity.

propositions.text: In 2000, organized crime members extorted 1,000 quetzals monthly from her and other merchants.
propositions.quote: On XXXX XXXX, 2000, the female claimant was contacted by telephone by some members of organized crime who asked her for 1,000 quetzals a month. In order to continue working, she had to pay this amount-this extortion was applied to all citizens who were merchants.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges organized crime extorted 1,000 quetzals monthly from her and other merchants in 2000.

propositions.text: She reported extortion to police who never appeared; her husband reported to public ministry which required timely reporting.
propositions.quote: She reported it by telephone so that the police would monitor the sector and catch the criminals. She stated that the police never appeared. The male claimant went to the public ministry to report it. It wanted him to report them at the time of the intimidation so that the authority could conduct an investigation.

propositions.text: Authorities said they could not protect her 24 hours a day.
propositions.quote: The authorities also stated that they were unable to protect the female claimant 24 hours a day.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges police did not respond to reports and authorities said they could not protect her continuously.

propositions.text: She collected signatures and led groups paying and not paying extortion, sending lists accusing authorities of complicity.
propositions.quote: To pressure the authorities, the female claimant collected signatures and written statements. She led the group that paid and the others who did not want to pay. The female claimant sent three lists to the police authorities-those who did not want to pay, those who paid, and the undecided. The last report accused the authorities of complicity in organized crime and declared them responsible and blamed them for the situation being experienced by the entire population.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges she led efforts to pressure authorities by collecting signatures and accusing them of complicity.

propositions.text: She moved to another sector to sell; criminal investigation officers came to her home to question her as an example.
propositions.quote: The female claimant moved to another sector of XXXX XXXX to continue to sell. On XXXX XXXX, 2000, some criminal investigation officers of the criminal investigation branch (DIC) came to her home because the female claimant had to respond to some offences before the authorities. They wanted to start with her to set an example for the entire population.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges she moved sectors and was questioned by criminal investigators to set an example.

propositions.text: She left the country to escape criminals and feared returning to the US due to employment.
propositions.quote: On XXXX XXXX, the female claimant left the country to be far from the criminals who wanted to stop her because of the reports. She feared returning to the United States because she was employed in her country of origin.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges she left the country to escape criminals and feared returning to the US due to employment.

propositions.text: Her husband returned to Guatemala in 2005 but left after threats; extortion calls continued forcing brother to relocate.
propositions.quote: In XXXX 2005, her husband XXXX XXXX XXXX, the male claimant, returned from the United States to Guatemala to obtain a work visa. He had to leave after one week. In fact, calls began in order to get revenge and to find out about the male claimant. After he left, the threatening calls extorting money continued, forcing his other brother to relocate.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges her husband returned briefly in 2005 but left due to threats; extortion calls continued affecting family.

propositions.text: The female claimant fears returning to Guatemala because of criminals.
propositions.quote: The female claimant fears returning to live in Guatemala because of the criminals.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges fear of returning to Guatemala due to criminals.

propositions.text: Exhibit A-2,1 with passports identifies claimants satisfactorily.
propositions.quote: Exhibit A-2,1, which includes photocopies of the claimants' passports, identifies them to the panel's satisfaction.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimants are satisfactorily identified by passport exhibits.

propositions.text: The testimony was not credible; the female claimant alleged extortionists disguised to avoid recognition.
propositions.quote: The testimony before the panel was not credible. It appeared that the female claimant was allegedly called and visited by the extortionist gangs, who were disguised in large glasses and hats so that they would not be recognized.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the testimony not credible, noting the claimant's claim of disguised extortionists.

propositions.text: The female claimant was a street vendor who also sold at clients' homes by visiting them.
propositions.quote: It became clear that the female claimant was a street vendor but that she also sold at clients' homes. She paid visits and offered her merchandise, which was purchased by volunteers.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant was a street vendor who also sold merchandise by visiting clients' homes.

propositions.text: The female claimant stated she received six calls between two dates in 2000, with extortionists forcing payment within three days.
propositions.quote: When asked about the calls received, she stated that she had received six calls in total. The first call allegedly took place on XXXX XXXX, 2000. The last call allegedly took place on XXXX XXXX, 2000. During that five-day period, some extortionists also went to the market to force her to pay 1,000 quetzals. She allegedly was given a time frame of three days to make the payment.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant stated she received six calls in 2000 and was forced to pay extortion within three days.

propositions.text: The panel and claimant situated calls as occurring three or four times a day.
propositions.quote: The panel, along with the female claimant, situated the calls that she received sometimes three or four times a day.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the calls were said to occur three or four times daily.

propositions.text: The claimant alleged calls on specific dates and times, including many calls on her cellphone.
propositions.quote: The second time, she allegedly received some calls on XXXX XXXX. The third time, on XXXX XXXX, she allegedly received the calls in the evening. The fourth time was on XXXX XXXX in the morning. The fifth time was on XXXX XXXX in the night; the sixth time was on XXXX XXXX-she allegedly received many calls, that is, ten calls or more, on her cellphone.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant alleged calls on specific dates and times, including many calls on her cellphone.

propositions.text: On a date in 2000, three individuals warned her; she went to police who told her to call when gang was present.
propositions.quote: Finally, on XXXX XXXX, 2000, three individuals approached her to inform her that it was the last warning. On XXXX XXXX, the female claimant went to the police. The police allegedly told her that she must call the police when the gang was present or call on her cell phone.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant was warned by three individuals and police told her to call when gang was present.

propositions.text: The female claimant gave inconsistent dates for the last call and later said she did not remember well.
propositions.quote: The female claimant was confronted with the calls and the dates. In one version, she allegedly declared that the last call occurred on the XXXX; later, the last call allegedly occurred on the XXXX. Finally, the female claimant allegedly declared that it was a long time ago and that she did not remember the dates well.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant gave inconsistent dates for the last call and later said she did not remember well.

propositions.text: It is normal to mistake dates after 12 years, but claimant earlier recalled details well.
propositions.quote: The panel recognizes that these events did indeed take place 12 years ago. It is normal and understandable for the female claimant to mistake a date. In her case, earlier on, she was able to remember not only the days but also the number of calls received and the time when the calls were received-if it was, for example, in the morning or the evening-or the number of calls received in the morning or the evening.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it normal to mistake dates after 12 years but claimant earlier recalled details well.

propositions.text: The panel rejects the dates given by the claimant as fabricated and not in her PIF.
propositions.quote: The panel does not accept the dates given by the female claimant. They are completely fabricated and are not in her PIF. In fact, whereas she stated that she received the last call on XXXX XXXX or XXXX, in her PIF, at paragraph 14, she wrote: [translation] "Because of the calls and fears, I moved to another sector of XXXX XXXX" on XXXX XXXX, 2000.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the claimant's dates as fabricated and inconsistent with her PIF.

propositions.text: Calls allegedly continued until XXXX XXXX, but testimony says calls stopped by XXXX or XXXX, 2000.
propositions.quote: That therefore implies that the calls allegedly continued until XXXX XXXX, whereas in her testimony, she allegedly received calls until XXXX XXXX or XXXX, 2000.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes calls allegedly continued until XXXX XXXX, but testimony says calls stopped by XXXX or XXXX, 2000.

propositions.text: There were about 30 days when the claimant did not receive calls; testimony and PIF differ on when calls stopped.
propositions.quote: Therefore, there were about 30 days when the female claimant did not receive calls at all. According to her story, during her hearing and in her PIF, the calls continued until the XXXX, and in her testimony at the hearing, the calls stopped on the XXXX or the XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds about 30 days without calls; claimant's story and testimony differ on when calls stopped.

propositions.text: Claimant's claim to mobilize merchants is implausible given her status as street vendor or home salesperson.
propositions.quote: Throughout her testimony, the female claimant tried to present herself as a female leader who allegedly mobilized the other merchants, as well as a torchbearer for the merchants there. It is implausible that the female claimant, who is a street vendor, or a home salesperson, was able to mobilize the merchants with stores to tell them not to pay the Maras.

propositions.text: More plausible that claimant mobilized other street or market vendors, not merchants with stores.
propositions.quote: It is more plausible that she would mobilize the other vendors at her level, that is, the street vendors, or market vendors and travelling salespeople, and not the merchants with stores.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's claim to mobilize merchants implausible; more plausible she mobilized street vendors.

propositions.text: Panel does not believe claimant was able to mobilize merchants as claimed.
propositions.quote: The panel does not believe that the female claimant was able to mobilize the merchants, as she claims.

paragraphs.summary: The panel disbelieves claimant's claim to mobilize merchants.

propositions.text: Claimant's testimony that she acted alone conflicts with PIF statement 'We sent...', indicating a group involvement.
propositions.quote: While she claimed in her testimony that she acted alone and that she went to the police alone, the female claimant was confronted with paragraph 12 of her PIF, in which she states: "We sent...". This "we" indicates a group of workers.

propositions.text: Claimant had no response to inconsistency about group involvement.
propositions.quote: The female claimant had no response to this inconsistency, in which it seems that it was a group of vendors who was working with her.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's testimony of acting alone conflicts with PIF indicating group involvement; claimant gave no response.

propositions.text: Even if credible, claimant faced generalized violence; documentary evidence shows extortion gangs demand ransoms from entire population.
propositions.quote: Even supposing that the story is credible, the female claimant faced generalized violence. The documentary evidence points out that the Maras or the extortionist gangs demand ransoms from the entire population.

propositions.text: Claim that claimant was targeted for reporting police or gangs is very general and not credible.
propositions.quote: The claim that she was targeted by the police or by the gangs, because she allegedly reported them, is very general. She is not credible.

propositions.text: Claimant stated police needed descriptions or names to proceed when called anonymously or when disguised extortionists appeared.
propositions.quote: In fact, the female claimant stated that, in order for the police to proceed, it needed the description of the people or the names of the criminals at the time when they called anonymously on the telephone and when they appeared disguised before the merchants.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant faced generalized violence; claim of targeting for reporting is general and not credible; police needed names to act.

propositions.text: Claimant never gave details to identify extortionists or crooked police officers allegedly colluding with gang.
propositions.quote: The female claimant never gave any detail to identify the extortionists or the crooked police officers who were allegedly in collusion with the gang of extortionists.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant never gave details to identify extortionists or corrupt police.

propositions.text: Since claimant did not identify responsible persons, panel does not believe criminal investigation officers came looking for her as claimed.
propositions.quote: Consequently, since she did not identify the people who were allegedly responsible for the wrongdoing towards her, the panel does not believe that criminal investigation branch officers came looking for the female claimant, as she claims in her PIF, because her report did not reveal any name.

paragraphs.summary: The panel disbelieves claimant's claim that criminal investigators came looking for her due to lack of identified names.

propositions.text: Claimant submitted documents reporting extortion but they do not identify anyone or enable arrest or vengeance.
propositions.quote: The female claimant submitted the documents that report the extortion; however, they do not identify anyone. The report does not identify the extortionist or their gang. It is general and does not enable any arrest; consequently, it also does not permit any vengeance.

propositions.text: Claimant talked about offenders in Exhibit A-2 but did not mention reporting them or the police.
propositions.quote: The female claimant was confronted with Exhibit A-2 (Form IMM-5611), in which she talked about offenders, but she did not mention anywhere that they reported them or the police.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant submitted extortion reports that do not identify offenders or mention reporting to police.

propositions.text: Claimant said no space to mention reporting police; panel rejects this explanation as inconsistent with other text.
propositions.quote: When confronted, she stated that she had not had space for it. The panel does not accept this explanation because in the text explaining her refugee protection claim she identified the problems with people being extorted on the buses; it is a very general description that does not concern her at all and that took more space than it would to state: "I reported the police and the criminals", or another short text of that kind that does not even taken up one line.

paragraphs.summary: The panel rejects claimant's explanation of no space to mention reporting police as inconsistent with other claim text.

propositions.text: Claimant's husband acknowledged fleeing to US due to extortionist gangs' threats while visiting ill mother in Guatemala.
propositions.quote: Concerning her husband, he acknowledged that when he was visiting his ill mother in Guatemala, he had to return to the United States urgently because the extortionist gangs indicated their intentions of coming to extort him. He allegedly fled to the United States.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant's husband fled to US due to extortion threats while visiting ill mother in Guatemala.

propositions.text: Claimants stayed in US for many years but did not claim refugee status due to illegal entry and missed deadlines.
propositions.quote: The claimants, who stayed in the United States for many years, ten years, did not claim refugee status because they had entered the United States illegally and they had exceeded the deadline for submitting their refugee protection claims within the time frame set out in the legislation.

propositions.text: Given all evidence, panel finds claimants failed to discharge burden of proof.
propositions.quote: Given all of the evidence, the panel is of the opinion that they claimants failed to discharge their burden of proof.

paragraphs.summary: Claimants stayed illegally in US without refugee claim; panel finds they failed to discharge burden of proof.

propositions.text: Designated representative did not submit evidence against US, son's country of citizenship.
propositions.quote: With respect to their son, the designated representative did not submit evidence against the United States, their son's country of citizenship.

paragraphs.summary: No evidence was submitted against the US, the son's country of citizenship.

propositions.text: Claimants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: Consequently, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, her spouse XXXX XXXX XXXX and their son XXXX XXXX XXXX are not "Convention refugees" or "persons in need of protection."

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes claimants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.
